title: Wealth and poverty
note: Latin pecunia, money, gives pecuniary (about money) and impecunious (without it). Generosity: munificent, largesse. Greed: avarice, rapacious, acquisitive. Thrift taken too far is parsimonious; spending taken too far is profligate. A windfall arrives unearned; an emolument is earned by holding a job or office.

items.a: having a great deal of money; wealthy
items.ex: The affluent suburb has three golf courses and no bus line.

items.a: ostentatiously rich and luxurious
items.ex: The opulent lobby was all marble, gold leaf and chandeliers.

items.a: splendid and expensive-looking
items.ex: The wedding ended with a sumptuous feast of seven courses.

items.a: very generous, especially in giving money
items.ex: A munificent alumna paid for the new library.

items.a: generous giving of money or gifts
items.ex: The town depended on the largesse of the mill's owner.

items.a: extremely unwilling to spend money
items.ex: The parsimonious landlord turned off the heat on April 1, snow or not.

items.a: extreme greed for wealth
items.ex: Avarice drove the miners to dig until the tunnel collapsed.

items.a: aggressively greedy or grasping
items.ex: Rapacious lenders charged the farmers ruinous interest.

items.a: eager to acquire and possess things
items.ex: An acquisitive collector, he owned four hundred clocks.

items.a: relating to money
items.ex: The director denied having any pecuniary interest in the deal.

items.a: to pay for services or work
items.ex: Jurors are remunerated at a modest daily rate.

items.a: a salary, fee, or profit from a job or office
d: a gift given out of charity
items.ex: The judge's emoluments included a house and a carriage.

items.a: producing a great deal of profit
items.ex: Selling bottled water at the stadium proved lucrative.

items.a: able to pay all one's debts
items.ex: A loan from his sister kept the shop solvent through winter.

items.a: unable to pay one's debts
items.ex: The airline was declared insolvent and grounded its fleet.

items.a: lacking the basic necessities of life
items.ex: The flood left hundreds of families destitute.

items.a: having little or no money
items.ex: The impecunious poet paid his rent in sonnets, or tried to.

items.a: extreme poverty
items.ex: He died in penury, though his paintings later sold for millions.

items.a: living by begging
items.ex: Mendicant friars depended on alms for food.

items.a: recklessly extravagant or wasteful
items.ex: The profligate heir spent a fortune on racehorses that never won.

items.a: to waste money or resources recklessly
items.ex: She squandered her lottery winnings within two years.

items.a: to steal money entrusted to one's care
d: to lend money at high interest
items.ex: The bookkeeper embezzled from the church fund for a decade.

items.a: lending money at excessively high interest
items.ex: Medieval law condemned usury as a sin.

items.a: a wealthy, powerful person in business
d: a person who lives by begging
items.ex: The railroad magnate built a mansion on Fifth Avenue.

items.a: an unexpected gain or piece of good fortune
items.ex: A tax refund was a windfall that paid for new tires.

items.a: unreasonably high, of a price or demand
items.ex: The airport charged an exorbitant twelve dollars for a sandwich.

items.a: money that is owed and overdue
items.ex: The tenants were three months in arrears on rent.

items.a: a benefit that comes with a job beyond salary
d: a debt owed to a lender
items.ex: A company car was one perquisite of the job.

items.a: wealth regarded as an evil influence or false god
items.ex: The preacher warned his flock against the worship of mammon.

items.a: to cut back on expenses
items.ex: Facing losses, the company retrenched, closing two plants.
